What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates,&nbsp; and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions.&nbsp; This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists.&nbsp; I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years.&nbsp;&nbsp; It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself.&nbsp; Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood.&nbsp; While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

Seven Takeaways on Convenience and News

Nieman Reports · 2026-09-25 14:53 UTC

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

Ten reported dead after two trains collide in Spain – latest updates

The Guardian · 2026-10-28 10:38 UTC

Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo Full report from Spain At least 10 people are feared to have died after two high-speed trains collided in the province of Toledo in Spain, with concerns the death toll could be much higher. The number of people affected is expected to rise, local authorities said, with growing concerns about a “major tragedy” ( 11:03 ). The affected trains are understood to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, making it 544 people in total on board of both train ( 10:46 ). The incident comes less than a year after a similar crash in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba, which killed 46 and injured 152 in January this year ( 11:00 ). Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, carrying 25 million passengers in 2024.

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

儿童手表“小天才圈”调查：点赞成每日功课，有商家可解除家长管控

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers amended school uniform regulations on September 21, prohibiting clothing "inconsistent with the principle of secular education." Although the regulations do not explicitly mention hijabs, schools began refusing entry to girls wearing headscarfs when the rules took effect on October 12. News reports showed distressed girls after being turned away from schools. Separate dress requirements adopted on October 6 also affected teachers. Authorities responded to the protests with widespread detentions.

Sudan: One Year on from the Cataclysm of El Fasher

Human Rights Watch · 2026-10-26 09:20 UTC

Click to expand Image Displaced women and girls walk through the vast IDP site in Tawila, Sudan, February 23rd, 2026. © 2026 Giles Clarke/Avaaz via Getty Images “It is as if a tsunami had hit the city,”&nbsp;said a resident who returned to Sudan’s El Fasher only to find it destroyed and largely abandoned after the Rapid Support Forces’ (RSF) October 2025 takeover. For 18 months, the RSF laid siege to the city, digging a trench around it in its final months, forcing starving residents to survive on animal fodder, until even that ran out.&nbsp; In the siege’s final weeks, the RSF increasingly used drones to target government soldiers, aligned armed groups, and civilians who were ensnared in a tiny area, leaving many maimed or dead.&nbsp; During the last days of the offensive, the RSF&nbsp;committed multiple massacres. The UN Human Rights Office&nbsp;estimates over 6,000 people were killed in just three days. RSF fighters also committed widespread sexual violence against women and girls and ran a massive abduction-for-ransom racket, killing those who couldn’t pay.

Coasian Stakeholder Theory -- by Matthew J. Higgins, Peter G. Klein, Anita McGahan, Rob Wuebker

NBER · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

Stakeholder theory asks who is in, who is out, and who gets what. Existing work illuminates important dimensions of firm–stakeholder relationships but does not supply a common, transaction-level rule connecting these questions. We use the Coase theorem to develop such a rule. A Coasian stakeholder is an actor with shutdown power, defined as the de facto capacity, within the relevant time horizon, to prevent, materially delay, or substantially reduce the expected joint value of a focal value-creating transaction. If all such actors are identified and bargaining and enforcement are costless, value-maximizing transactions proceed, although rights and bargaining positions may affect who captures value. When transaction costs are positive, however, identification, bargaining, coalition formation, and enforcement can delay, distort, or suppress those transactions.

Behavioral Finance at 40 -- by Nicholas C. Barberis

NBER · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

Behavioral finance seeks to improve our understanding of markets, investors, and firms by adopting a psychologically realistic description of how people think. While behavioral finance ideas have been part of human discourse for decades if not centuries, the modern research effort in the field began in the 1980s. Forty years later, behavioral finance is a vibrant area of financial economics. In this article, I explain why by reviewing some of its recent progress. I focus on three topics – beliefs about future earnings, beliefs about future returns, and prospect theory – and on their applications to understanding asset prices and investor behavior. I close by commenting on some new directions in the field – cognitive foundations, non-traditional decision processes, and artificial intelligence.

Governments invoke national security to regulate foreign acquisitions of domestic firms. Why is ownership regulation a distinct policy margin beyond standard tools, like production subsidies and trade taxes? We show that contractual frictions make multinational firm boundaries central to geoeconomic policy. Within firms, ownership allocates residual control that affects outcomes through non-contractible decisions. Between governments, the absence of enforceable agreements makes the economic costs of conflict shape geopolitical bargaining. It can increase foreign dependence, technology transfer, or sabotage scope. If such margins were contractible, the government could regulate them directly. Tariff Staggering -- by Stephanie Schmitt-Grohé, Martín Uribe

NBER · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

Using a panel of U.S. imports and customs duties at the HS 6-digit level, we document that in a typical quarter about 20 percent of tariffs rise, 20 percent fall, and 60 percent remain unchanged. Motivated by these facts, we develop a model of staggered tariff setting and embed it in a dynamic open-economy framework. Staggering changes the dynamics of the cross-sectional mean tariff, generating hump-shaped macroeconomic responses to tariff shocks. Staggering also overturns the Razin–Svensson trade- balance neutrality result for permanent tariff increases, because the gradual adjustment of the mean tariff creates an anticipation effect that induces agents to front-load net imports. Inherited tariff dispersion has first-order macroeconomic effects, allowing tariff harmonization to be studied with linear approximation methods. We find that eliminating tariff dispersion while holding the mean tariff unchanged has effects akin to a transitory tariff cut in an economy without staggering.

Ratings, Debt, and Deficits: An Exploration -- by Olivier J. Blanchard, Daniel Leigh, Prachi Mishra

NBER · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

We look at the effects of debt and primary fiscal balances on sovereign credit ratings through the lens of a simple model. We find that the ratings differ from the implications of the model in three important ways. They give much more weight to debt relative to forecast primary balances. They understate the effects of the difference between the interest rate and the growth rate. They give a very large role to country effects. For the same level of debt and forecast primary balances, they imply extremely different ratings across countries, and imply extremely different levels of debt needed to reach a given rating.

The Impact of Silver Loading in ACA Health Insurance Marketplaces -- by Coleman Drake, David Anderson, Dylan Nagy, Mark Shepard

NBER · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

In 2017, the federal government ended payments for cost-sharing reduction (CSR) subsidies for the Health Insurance Marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act. Rather than uniformly increase Marketplace plans’ premiums to offset the loss of these payments, over 40 states responded by silver loading—only increasing the premiums of silver plans to which CSR subsidies apply and premium tax credits are tied. Silver loading was intended to increase the affordability of Marketplace coverage by increasing premium tax credits and thereby enrollment, though the literature lacks causal estimates. Furthermore, Congress is considering reinstating CSR subsidy funding, effectively undoing silver loading. We use panel data on 2015-2021 Marketplace health plan premiums and enrollment in 12 states from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to estimate silver loading’s effects using contiguous county-pair models.

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-28 00:00 UTC

The 20th century shift from sterling to the dollar is often cited as evidence that currency dominance is not forever. This column presents a nonlinear model of the international monetary system calibrated on historical events. Shifts in dominance require large, simultaneous combinations of shocks, with democracy and conflicts playing a central role. Stress tests suggest that dollar dominance is resilient: a decline would require repeated shocks in the US alongside major reforms in China and Europe. Parallels between the dollar’s rise in the 20th century and that of the renminbi in the 21st century should be treated with extreme caution.

Not your average firm: Heterogeneous cross-border financial allocations

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-28 00:00 UTC

International financial integration is often measured through national totals. Yet these totals can conceal very different experiences across firms. Using comprehensive French microdata, this column shows that most financially internationalised firms raise foreign equity without investing abroad, while a small group of large firms dominates cross-border positions. Foreign funding is associated with greater equity financing, lower bank debt, and higher investment. This heterogeneity also means that aggregate estimates understate the importance of country factors for the cross-border allocations of the typical firm.

Adult social care can be better value than the health care we already fund

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-27 00:00 UTC

Health programmes must clear cost-effectiveness thresholds, but social care faces no such test. This column uses Spain's 2007 long-term care reform to show that access to cash subsidies and publicly funded home help raised life satisfaction, reduced loneliness, and increased survival, at a cost per quality-adjusted life year well below the thresholds applied to health programmes. The results suggest that part of a national care service could be funded by replacing less cost-effective health programmes with social care.

How agreements between suppliers and retailers can weaken competition

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-27 00:00 UTC

Agreements between manufacturers and retailers can affect competition across brands and stores. This column documents retail price patterns in the US consumer battery industry and uses a model estimated from purchase data to explore two potential mechanisms: changes in downstream retail pricing and changes in upstream wholesale contracting. Counterfactual simulations illustrate how these mechanisms could jointly weaken competition. In the scenarios examined, the wholesale channel generates the larger consumer welfare loss. The findings highlight the importance of considering both channels when evaluating the potential effects of vertical agreements.

Private equity beyond the target: How buyouts reshape supply chains

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-10-26 00:00 UTC

The importance of private equity for euro area firms is increasing, with annual growth rates in assets under management exceeding 10%. Private equity buyouts affect more than just the firms being acquired. Using comprehensive data for Belgium, this column shows that the sales volumes of suppliers grow faster when there is a higher proportion of business with customers backed by private equity. But this advantage is lost during downturns, as investors push for cost savings. Buyouts can also crowd out competitors that depend on the same suppliers. Finally, high leverage implies greater interest rate sensitivity, so private equity buyouts can intensify the transmission of monetary policy to target firms and beyond.

Failures in Gemini Context Retrieval I have a 730 page Word document which records the verbatim dialogue between myself and an AI collaborator on a project on antique jewellery over many weeks. We agreed the protocol that I would save the conversation in Word and upload it at the start of each session to ensure continuity in the project and overcome any 'memory' limits. These five divisions define how far we can go in space

Big Think · 2026-10-28 06:00 UTC

In this Universe, just because you can see it doesn&#8217;t mean you can reach it. Conversely, just because you can&#8217;t see it today doesn&#8217;t necessarily mean that its light won&#8217;t arrive tomorrow. Because the fabric of the Universe itself is expanding, and because the maximum speed at which any signal — whether massive or massless — can travel through that fabric of space is finite, there are both: places that we can currently see that we could never reach or communicate with, and places that we cannot currently observe today, but whose light is on the way and will someday reach us in the future. Today, there&#8217;s a well-understood limit for how far we can observe in any direction in space: 46.1 billion light-years.

Generalized CliqueBots in Open-Source Game Theory

LessWrong · 2026-10-28 05:59 UTC

In this post, I suggest the notion of an interface-relative CliqueBot in open-source game theory. Such a bot cooperates only with the likes of it – from the point of view of a finite number of probing functions. There are several reasons the notion could be valuable. First, it suggests a perspective where programs are secondary to the interface they use – or at least are to be regarded in the context of this interface. This helps put existing bots within one coherent picture and points to their deeper nature. Second, it provides a factory for new bots; I illustrate how it gives rise to many existing and some arguably new ones. Moreover, properties of CliqueBots can perhaps be used to define or study the properties of the corresponding interfaces. The first sections provide an overview; new material starts from Section 3. 1. Program games In classic game theory, players commit to actions . Program games add a new layer to this: instead of submitting their actions directly, players submit programs to act on their behalf.

The missing ingredient of AI consciousness

LessWrong · 2026-10-28 04:19 UTC

In his book The Feeling of What Happens , Antonio Damasio offers a neurobiological theory of consciousness. Things happen to every object, but consciousness, he argues, emerges when there is an acknowledgement that it is to me that these things are happening. In this framework, consciousness is the recognition that there is a you, that things are happening to you, and that, because of this, you have changed. Specifically, Damasio states that “consciousness is the part of mind concerned with the apparent sense of self and knowing” ( Damasio, 1999 , p. 27). Importantly, this framework distinguishes feeling from knowing. Feelings and emotions emerged as regulatory states to help animals fulfill their evolutionary goals, but before consciousness, the owner of these emotions was oblivious to them. Consciousness arises as the feeling of a feeling, that is, being aware of one’s feelings. In summary, Damasio’s model of consciousness begins with a proto-self: an interconnected coherent collection of neural patterns that represent the state of the organism, moment by moment.

Great but Painful

LessWrong · 2026-10-28 03:38 UTC

If you want to build a product that people will use, find something that people already do and make it less painful. People are notoriously bad at knowing what they want. If you ask someone what they want then they will typically tell you what they think a socially virtuous person is expected to want. They will tell you that they want to eat healthier, understand people with different political opinions, know whether news stories are reliable, make more friends, be a better parent, and serve their community. Silicon Valley is littered with the graves of products that tried to solve problems users said they wanted to solve. These products typically got enthusiastic responses when shown to users, and the developers were surprised to see them get little usage after they were launched. In practice, the biggest sign that a user will use a product is that they already do the thing the product lets them do, and gain a clear benefit from doing so, but the current way they do it is painful. Pretty much all successful consumer tech products succeeded by following this formula.

The world hasn’t become less smelly — we’ve just lost our nasal knowledge

Big Think · 2026-10-27 14:30 UTC

Air, land, and sea. Our world is characterized by a proliferating variety of uncertain scents. Yet our noses are ill-equipped to discern between them. Pollution, pandemics, and poverty have conspired to reduce our sensitivity. Some gases, such as the rotten-egg stink of hydrogen sulfide emitted by industries and waste sites, induce a selective loss of smell. These substances are most dangerous when they are least odorous. When we try to use our noses, the result can be confusion. Supermarkets across the globe have begun to remove “best before” dates from products such as milk and yogurt in an attempt to avoid food waste. They have encouraged consumers to deploy the sniff test to distinguish the sweet, mild, scent of fresh milk from a sour spoiled odor. Sniffing was one of the main ways in which premodern people could discern the freshness of food; but thanks to the arrival of cellophane packaging and refrigeration, we have allowed our nasal knowledge to deteriorate.

Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist turns to one of philosophy&#8217;s oldest questions: what is consciousness, and where does it come from? He argues the brain doesn&#8217;t create consciousness — it shapes it, the way a larynx shapes air into a voice, filtering a larger field of consciousness into something distinctly yours. From there he builds toward panpsychism, the idea that consciousness pervades everything, from single-cell organisms to mountains. Along the way, he uses the image of a whirlpool in a stream to explain how a stable &#8220;self&#8221; can exist within constant flow, and makes the case that matter itself is simply a phase of consciousness. Do the three quantum forces all unify together?

Big Think · 2026-10-27 06:00 UTC

Here in our Universe, there are a series of fundamental forces that all appear to operate independently of one another. There&#8217;s gravity, which is an attractive force between all objects with mass and/or energy, governed by Einstein&#8217;s general relativity and the curvature of spacetime. There&#8217;s electromagnetism, where any particle with an electric charge or an electric or magnetic field is affected by other charges and electromagnetic fields in the environment. There&#8217;s the weak nuclear force, which enables particles to change species and to decay from a heavier species into a lighter one. And there&#8217;s the strong nuclear force, which holds atomic nuclei together and binds quarks (and antiquarks) together into hadrons. We aren&#8217;t sure whether gravity is an inherently quantum force or not, but the other three forces — electromagnetism , the weak nuclear force , and the strong nuclear force — all have quantum field theories that describe them.

You have more control over reality than you think

Big Think · 2026-10-26 13:00 UTC

Is a “red” rose really red?&nbsp; According to Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, it’s not that simple. While the flower may appear obviously red, the color isn’t an inherent property of the flower itself. Instead, it’s relational, meaning it emerges from the relationship between light, receptors in the eye, and signals processed in the brain. So, if something as basic as color depends on the relationship between the world and the person perceiving it, what about the rest of reality?&nbsp; This thought exercise reveals how each of us contributes to our reality, Barrett says, and how we have more control — more responsibility — than we might think. Seeing the same world differently&nbsp; Barrett uses animals to break down the concept. Humans typically have three types of color receptors, or cones, in the retina, while dogs have only two. Because of this, we may see a rose as red while a dog sees it as muddy brown. We might assume the dog simply can’t see the rose’s “true” red color.

Tender Buttons

MUBI Notebook · 2026-10-27 08:00 UTC

One Sings, the Other Doesn't (Agnès Varda, 1977). In her memoir, Varda par Agnès , the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe ( Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex ), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two women: “Qu’est ce qu’être femme?” While showing a naked female infant rolling around on its back, the reply comes in her voiceover: “To be born a woman means being born with female genitals.” The next shot is of a blond adult female, naked and standing up, saying, “To be a woman means inhabiting a woman’s body.

More Visible Abroad than at Home: Nigeria’s New Art Cinema and the Country that Can’t Screen It

MUBI Notebook · 2026-10-26 08:00 UTC

My Father's Shadow (Akinola Davies Jr., 2025). In Lagos last September, a handful of screenings of My Father’s Shadow (2025) played in theaters that were, depending on the night, half empty. A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions. Despite all these nominations and recognitions, Nigerian audiences barely registered the film. I don’t think most Nigerians who heard about the Cannes win ever connected it to an actual cinema outing. But what is notable about this isn’t the story of one film not finding a local audience.

Issue 9 of Notebook invites readers to journey through the intertwined histories of magic and cinema, uncovering screen wonders both spiritual and secular. Hollywood consultants behind productions including Sinners and Hugo break down how witchcraft, Hoodoo, and performance magic is represented onscreen.

Masao Adachi: Demystifying a Legend

MUBI Notebook · 2026-10-20 08:00 UTC

Masao Adachi in 2025. Photograph by David Matthew Davis. Masao Adachi is a filmmaker whose reputation well and truly precedes him. Born in 1939 in Kyushu, Japan, he moved to Tokyo to attend Nihon University, coming of age during the turbulent protests against the renewal of the mutual security treaty between Japan and the United States in 1959–60. He started making films with a student group and soon emerged as one of the leading figures in the burgeoning underground cinema scene. In the mid-1960s, Adachi became involved with the sexploitation industry, writing and directing several striking examples of the genre for Koji Wakamatsu’s production company. He was also collaborating with major members of the New Wave like Nagisa Oshima. The political dimension to his output became more explicit in the early 1970s, following a visit to Lebanon, where he filmed Palestinian guerrillas.

Against The Grain: Metal resistance

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC

As far right ideology and misogyny make gains around the world, metal, a subculture with a troubled relationship to fascism, wonders whether more progressive ideals are still in reach, writes Antonio Poscic in The Wire 513 Metal used to be the music of outsiders. For teenagers who stumbled into it, the subculture offered a place to belong and legitimised intense emotions that had to be suppressed in daily life. Its lyrics and sonic density gave shape to alienation, despair and angst that many struggled to articulate. It offered acceptance for those rejected elsewhere, and an identity chosen rather than imposed. As sociologist Deena Weinstein&rsquo;s research in the 1990s showed, metal circles often acted as scaffolding for adolescent development. Today, other subcultures have become fragmented by the internet and streaming, but metal remains a counterexample, perhaps precisely because of the strong sense of belonging on which it was built.

AD—WO to Renovate the Heinz Architectural Center at Pittsburgh’s Carnegie Museum of Art

ArchDaily · 2026-10-28 05:30 UTC

Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum of Art has commissioned architecture and urban design practice AD—WO to reimagine the Heinz Architectural Center . The practice, led by Emanuel Admassu and Jen Wood and one of the winners of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards , was recognized for exploring relationships among people, place, history and material culture, bringing an interdisciplinary approach to the architecture experience. The Heinz Architectural Center is the museum's forum to present, explore and incubate architectural ideas, currently located in the institution's main building, which dates from 1907. The new design aims to transform the Center into a contemporary facility that brings together exhibitions, collections, research, learning and public engagement. AD—WO is working with R3A as architect of record, Buro Happold for engineering and sustainability, Tillotson Design Associates for lighting and VizzAcoustics for acoustics.

Inhabiting as Inquiry: Threads from the 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial

ArchDaily · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

Inhabiting a space involves multiple economic, social, cultural, geographic, political, and environmental factors. Beyond these considerations, however, it engages with processes, boundaries, and possibilities that have repeatedly become subjects of architectural inquiry. "We are builders of a society," declared Solano Benitez during his lecture titled The Place of Architecture at the Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial. Through a series of international lectures, exhibitions across different locations in the city, and activities open to all generations, the 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial examined the value of inhabitation, recognizing architecture as the discipline that gives meaning to how and where we live and, consequently, how we exist within society.

[Series] Governing the digital determinants of health for children and young people: a global public health imperative

The Lancet · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

The digital determinants of health are the structural conditions through which digital infrastructures, business models, and design choices shape health outcomes. Yet these determinants remain largely outside public health policy and remain fragmented across regulatory sectors. Rather than regulating individual technologies in isolation, governance should ensure that digital systems and environments advance population health and reduce inequities. A public health approach shifts attention from individual responsibility—and the tendency to blame users—towards the governance of the structural features that produce health risks and inequities.

The Lancet · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

Children and adolescents are growing up in a hybrid world in which digital media has become part of the infrastructure of everyday life and a structural determinant of their health. In the second paper of this Series on the digital determinants of health, we apply the framework introduced in the first paper to one of the most contested questions in public health: how young people's digital media use shapes their health and wellbeing. Using the digital determinants of health framework to interpret the current evidence base, we examine what is known, and what remains poorly understood, about the public health implications of children's and adolescents’ digital media use.

journal · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

[Series] The digital determinants of health: a new era for global public health

The Lancet · 2026-10-28 10:56 UTC

Digital transformations exert increasing influence over the lives of the global population, shaping opportunities and generating harms for health and wellbeing across the spectrum of digital access and engagement. The scale of influence of digital transformations on human and planetary health marks the urgency of attention to the digital determinants of health (DDoH). In this Series paper, we describe a prevailing digital sociotechnological order (DSTO) as the structural source of the DDoH. The DSTO is composed of a set of dominant assumptions that motivate digital practices operating through four features (political norms, economic logics, infrastructures, and personal and social practices) to affect human and planetary health.

Spacetime Sentinels: a Qiskit game that exposes the competition between spacetime checks and magic in low-overhead quantum error detection

arXiv · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.35924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Spacetime Sentinels, a game in which the player protects a noisy circuit with spacetime Pauli checks and is scored on the post-selected fidelity and the fraction of shots that survive, with every number computed in Qiskit. The player spends a budget of ancilla qubits on checks found by the qiskit-paulice add-on, must inject a quota of $T$ gates into the protected circuit, and chooses whether to place them where they commute with every check or to ignore the checks. Each move is evaluated exactly with Qiskit Aer density-matrix simulation against a stabilizer or statevector reference, and the evaluation agrees with 50,000-shot runs of the SamplerV2 primitive. We score moves with a fidelity rate $R=F_{\mathrm{ps}}\kappa^{1/2}$, whose inverse square is the sampling overhead of detection followed by rescaling. Exhaustive evaluation of all 5,412 legal moves under two noise models, together with sweeps over five random payloads, reveals three trade-offs that are not obvious before playing.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Accelerating fits in high-energy physics and beyond

arXiv · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.35927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data analysis in particle physics often involves optimizing a loss function that quantifies how well a theoretical model describes the observed data, in order to estimate the parameters of the model. This is referred to as fitting. As datasets grow larger and more expensive analysis methods are used, the time required to perform this parameter estimation can be a limiting factor. This work explores techniques that can significantly accelerate the fitting process, and measures their performance on a set of example models chosen to be representative of a variety of physics fits. We compare the speed and precision of variants of several well-known optimization algorithms, namely Newton's method, BFGS, and the Migrad algorithm (commonly used in physics fits). We observe significant speedups when using some algorithms: most notably, some variants of BFGS are consistently about $10\times$ faster than Migrad across our benchmarks, while achieving the same precision.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

What We Could Lose by Trying to Make Mars Habitable

arXiv · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.35937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent push to develop Mars terraforming technologies, increasingly driven by unaccountable private wealth, risks the irreversible destruction of planetary records we have barely begun to read. In this sense, terraforming Mars would be akin to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria. Echoing Carl Sagan's words about the library, in this piece we argue that we should not let such an extensive loss of information happen again. As terraforming Mars would melt and destroy the icy record on Mars, we suggest closing an important gap in the COSPAR planetary protection framework, by expanding regulations on preventing biological contamination to preventing large-scale atmospheric modification and destruction of cryospheric and geologic records.

arXiv:2610.35951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observations of high-redshift galaxies from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) provide a complementary probe of early structure formation. We find that JWST has little impact on the parameter constraints of $\Lambda$CDM and HDE but produces more pronounced changes in those of IHDE. For CMB+DESI+DES-Dovekie, adding JWST shifts the holographic parameter $c$ from $1.270^{+0.146}_{-0.096}$ to $1.091\pm0.095$ and the interaction parameter $\beta$ from $0.650^{+0.104}_{-0.034}$ to $0.498^{+0.090}_{-0.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Walk on Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable and Composable Transport Medium Prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE Solvers

arXiv · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.35952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials. We introduce Walk on Multiscale Media (WoMM), which compiles fine-scale transport into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs. A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions retaining fine-scale material effects. Each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, enabling incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion. Integrated with conventional Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous--discrete solver, these prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem.

Dynamical systems analysis of Bianchi type-IX cosmology with a scalar field mediated dark sector interaction

arXiv · 2026-10-28 04:00 UTC

arXiv:2610.35953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent DESI DR2 results preference for a time-varying dark-energy equation of state, together with the long-standing difficulty of explaining why an initially anisotropic universe should evolve toward isotropy, motivates the study of interacting dark-sector models in anisotropic backgrounds. We investigate the dynamics of Bianchi type-IX cosmologies containing pressureless dark matter coupled to dark energy in the form of a quintessence scalar field $\phi$ with exponential potential $V(\phi)=V_0\,e^{-\lambda\phi}$. Energy exchange between the two dark components is mediated by the scalar field through the interaction term $Q=\kappa\beta\dot\phi\,\rho_{\rm DM}$, where $\kappa^2=8\pi G$ and $\beta$ is a dimensionless coupling. Because Bianchi~IX models generically recollapse, the Hubble scalar $H$ vanishes at the moment of maximum expansion, where the expansion-normalized variables of the standard Wainwright--Ellis formalism diverge.

Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes

Phys.org Mollusks · 2026-10-20 13:30 UTC

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture

Microsoft Research Blog · 2026-10-21 16:00 UTC

For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. Why pipes sometimes get "stuck": buffering

Let&rsquo;s say you&rsquo;re running this command to watch for some specific output in a log file: tail -f /some/log/file | grep thing1 | grep thing2 If log lines are being added to the file relatively slowly, the result I&rsquo;d see is&hellip; nothing! It doesn&rsquo;t matter if there were matches in the log file or not, there just wouldn&rsquo;t be any output. I internalized this as &ldquo;uh, I guess pipes just get stuck sometimes and don&rsquo;t show me the output, that&rsquo;s weird&rdquo;, and I&rsquo;d handle it by just running grep thing1 /some/log/file | grep thing2 instead, which would work. So as I&rsquo;ve been doing a terminal deep dive over the last few months I was really excited to finally learn exactly why this happens. why this happens: buffering The reason why &ldquo;pipes get stuck&rdquo; sometimes is that it&rsquo;s VERY common for programs to buffer their output before writing it to a pipe or file.

The Conductor Developer

Martin Fowler · 2026-10-28 10:57 UTC

TL;DR Why I think software development is starting to feel a little more like conducting an orchestra. There’s a shift happening in software development that I don’t think we’re talking about clearly enough. For the last couple of years we’ve framed AI as a productivity tool. How much faster can it write code? How many more features can we ship? How much cheaper can we build software? I think that’s the wrong question, but I understand why. The first thing AI became good at was writing code, so naturally that’s where we focused. As AI got better at coding, I expected the bottlenecks to move through the software delivery lifecycle: from coding to design and specification, architecture, then verification. And they have. We spent a lot of time at the most recent FOSE event discussing how we ensure good design, quality and resilience while agents increasingly write the code. That’s a topic for another ramble. A few months ago, though, I realised I was looking at the wrong bottleneck. I kept assuming it would simply move to the next phase of software delivery. I was wrong.

333 Tor Exit Nodes Hijacked To Intercept SSH Traffic And Retrieve Plaintext Email

SoylentNews · 2026-10-28 10:57 UTC

https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2026/10/300-tor-exit-nodes-hijacked-to-intercept-ssh-traffic-and-retrieve-plaintext-email/ Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn't find among Switzerland2's authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.

[$] Python's experimental JIT to be removed

LWN.net · 2026-10-26 15:45 UTC

Python's experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler , which was added to CPython in 2024 for the 3.13&#160;release , is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council announced that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an accepted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating PEP&#160;836 ("JIT Go Brrr: The Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython") to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on the once-promising project has come to an end.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group . The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version . Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions .

Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-26 17:04 UTC

By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive , an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro . It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-23 18:32 UTC

By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-22 22:19 UTC

Samartha Chandrashekar &amp; Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run.

The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode . Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1 . Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true , so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file , but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy . Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support . If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

Kubernetes v1.37: Tracking When a PersistentVolumeClaim Was Last Used (Beta)

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-09-21 18:30 UTC

Kubernetes v1.37 promotes the PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature gate to Beta (enabled by default). With this feature, the PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) protection controller adds an Unused condition to each PVC, telling you whether any running pod currently references it — no custom tooling or cross-referencing required. For the API definition of PVC conditions, see the PersistentVolumeClaim API reference . Read on to learn how the Unused condition works and how to use it. Why track PVC usage? In large-scale Kubernetes clusters, it is common for users to create PVCs and then delete the associated pods without cleaning up the storage, because Kubernetes does not automatically delete PVCs when their pods are removed (to protect against accidental data loss). Over time, these orphaned PVCs may accumulate, silently consuming storage capacity and driving up cloud costs. Before Kubernetes v1.37, it was easy to identify an unused PersistentVolume, but much harder to determine whether a PVC was still being used.

In a lab in Luxembourg in 2024, engineers at Flawless Photonics unpacked a spool of glass fiber that had just returned from the International Space Station (ISS). As they threaded it onto their rewinding machine, the machine jammed—as happens sometimes—and they braced for the usual outcome: The fiber would snap. This time, though, nothing broke. It was an early hint that their experiment might have been successful. The Flawless Photonics team had set out to draw fibers of a heavy-metal fluoride glass called ZBLAN—named for its other components of zirconium, barium, lanthanum, aluminum, and sodium (chemical symbol Na)—in microgravity, aiming to achieve superior optical and physical properties. “We realized, wow, that fiber is much stronger than the stuff we had produced on Earth,” says Hubert Moser , the company’s cofounder and CTO. At Firefly Aerospace in Texas, engineers have been doing what NASA’s chief, Jared Isaacman, likes to call “the near-impossible.” The Firefly team has been assembling Blue Ghost Mission 2 , a robotic spacecraft intended to land on the far side of the moon in 2027. No U.S. spacecraft has ever gone there. Not very many have landed on the near side, either, for that matter. Blue Ghost 2 has thousands of potential failure points, and there is almost no room for error. Two ships sent by a competitor, Houston-based Intuitive Machines , reached the moon’s near side in 2024 and 2025 but fell over on landing and returned little useful data. In 2024, another mission, Peregrine Mission One , by Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technology , missed the moon entirely because a single helium valve wouldn’t seat properly. In summary: Moon landings are supremely hard. So far, since Project Apollo ended in 1972, U.S. spacecraft have landed intact exactly…once.

In addition to targeting the South Pole-Aitken Basin , NASA is eyeing lunar caves as a potential site for habitats and other lunar facilities. Meanwhile, space agencies need to send large amounts of cargo and robotic explorers to the surface. This includes the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation (GIMLI), a Planetary Science Institute –led proposal that will investigate a “skylight,” or a hole in an old lunar lava tube, to see if a large cave system extends beyond it . Such a location could provide a safe place for astronauts to operate on the surface in the future. The mission team will be led by Than Putzig , an associate director and senior scientist at PSI.

Since the discovery of the first remnants of a jet-powered Shahed drone near Kyiv in June 2025, these upgraded kamikaze UAVs have become a nightmare for Ukrainian civilians. Described by some analysts as the most significant Russian drone innovation since the beginning of the war, these uncrewed aerial vehicles are outrunning the beleaguered nation’s innovative interceptor systems, forcing a pivot in technology development and air-defense strategies. Russia manufactures the Iran-designed long-range Shahed drones , under the name Geran at its Yelabuga factory in Tatarstan, some 800 kilometers east of Moscow. In a little over a year, Russian engineers have developed three iterations of the jet-powered killer drone— Geran-3 , 4, and 5. Geran-3 , although fitted with a Chinese-made Telefly JT80 turbojet engine that enabled it to reach speeds of up to 370 kilometers per hour, was not very maneuverable and for that reason not much more effective than the propeller-powered Geran-2 .

Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-10-27 16:14 UTC

This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

IEEE Spectrum · 2026-10-27 13:00 UTC

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager.

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer . All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models

Schneier on Security · 2026-10-28 10:57 UTC

This is a problem: Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it&#8217;s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it&#8217;s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what&#8217;s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model&#8217;s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries &#8220;no&#8221; and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it&#8217;s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you&#8217;ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI&#8217;s gpt-oss...

Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs

Schneier on Security · 2026-10-28 10:57 UTC

Interesting research : Abstract : Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it.

French Court’s Site-Blocking Orders Drive Quad9 Out Of France

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-10-27 16:19 UTC

A nonprofit service that protects internet users’ privacy is leaving France. Quad9, a free DNS resolver, has said it will reluctantly stop serving users in France on November 24. This follows a French court order that Quad9 must block access to websites that are accused of infringing the copyrights of a sports broadcaster. Forcing a responsible privacy service out of an important market is a predictable result of trying to force infrastructure providers to be copyright police. When you visit a website, a DNS resolver reads the domain name you type in—like eff.org — and translates it into a numerical IP address that’s used to direct data across the internet. A DNS resolver can see the names of websites you connect to, so its privacy policies are important. Quad9 is an NGO that’s incorporated in Switzerland, in part to protect its users from data demands. The company also helps protect users from malware and phishing by blocking domains that are known to be malicious.

specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Lessons Learned From 'AdFection' and What To Do Next

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-10-26 17:28 UTC

Last week, researchers at Citizen Lab revealed a horrifying new malware campaign, dubbed “AdFection.” It used an ad network to distribute spyware to journalist’s devices to infect them without the target ever needing to click anything. This sort of attack on journalists is dangerous and incredibly concerning, especially since it’s built on the backbone of a technology we already object to: behavioral advertising . Although this type of attack has only been described targeting journalists, you can take a few steps we outline in the next section to mitigate the risk no matter who you are. A few factors combined to make this attack a noteworthy first-of-its-kind. First, it utilized the surveillance ad-tech ecosystem to specially target the malicious code. Second, the spyware it delivered was so-called “zero-click,” meaning it required no interaction from the user to be infected: all that is required is for the ad to be delivered and code bundled along with it to be run, which happens automatically. Neither malvertising nor zero-click attacks are new on their own.

Anti-Circumvention Laws Raise the Cost of Knowledge

Electronic Frontier Foundation · 2026-10-26 17:20 UTC

The vast amount of information on the open web requires researchers and journalists to adapt with new tools to make sense of it all. Checking facts, gauging public opinion, and other lines of inquiry depend on being able to analyze the overwhelming amount of material posted online every day. Unfortunately, responding to the AI industry’s voracious appetite for data, companies stewarding this public data are looking to cash in and block access to the open web. This makes the web harder to navigate, and threatens all kinds of important research. Reddit’s lawsuit against SerpAPI[1] and Perplexity threatens to do exactly that. Reddit was once a very open platform, fostering a community of alternative apps and extensions putting users in control of their experience. Since the rise of AI however, it changed tack. Over the last three years Reddit has closed APIs to users , limited UI features , and otherwise restrained access without login .

The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source

If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week — and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet . You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do? To find out what you can personally do read the first blog post in this series! What Is PHP? PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

Out Now: Low-tech Magazine Volume IV

Image: Low-tech Magazine Volume IV (2022-2026). Photo: Juliette Demaret. Low-tech Magazine presents the fourth volume in the chronological book series. It contains twenty articles that were published online between 2022 and 2026. Three earlier volumes collect articles written and published online between 2007 and 2021, which are also bundled in the &ldquo; Compressed Edition &rdquo;. This new volume is a bit different from the earlier books: eight of the articles are DIY guides or manuals, and we have grouped them together in the second part of the book. This volume covers the period that Marie Verdeil joined Low-tech Magazine, which partly shifted the focus from writing articles to building prototypes inspired by historical research. These prototypes also led us to conduct workshops in universities and participate in museum exhibitions. As is the case with all of our books, the articles have been edited and improved compared to the original web versions. Some articles gained extra or better images.

specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe

Rediscovering the Handcart

Low-Tech Magazine · 2026-04-22 00:00 UTC

Image: The handcart, equipped with a sail. Photo by Kris De Decker. The human-powered handcart is the oldest of vehicles, and it will likely be the last one around in the future. Of all vehicles, it&rsquo;s the cheapest and least complex to build and use. It offers a large advantage over carrying a load on your back or dragging it over the ground - the even older concept of the sled. On the other hand, the handcart is cheaper and easier to use than the animal-powered cart. Oxen and donkeys eat more than humans, and they have their own will, which can work against the driver. Like any other wheeled vehicle, the handcart requires roads to drive on. This infrastructure has not always been available anywhere or at any time in history. For example, in medieval Europe, porters and pack animals were more common than handcarts because of poor roads. 1 In the West, the handcart only reached its heyday during the first decades of the Industrial Revolution, when it connected fast-growing cities to train stations and harbors.

Low-tech Magazine: The Uncompressed Book Series

Low-Tech Magazine · 2026-03-30 00:00 UTC

Image: The redesigned and revised chronological book edition. Photo: Marie Verdeil. Between 2019 and 2021, Low-tech Magazine published three books containing selections of articles from the website, spanning 14 years (2007-2021). In 2024, we launched the &ldquo;compressed edition&rdquo; , which squeezes the article catalog of the three-volume book series into just one book of 620 pages. We did this by switching to a smaller font size, downsizing most images, and opting for a two-column layout. I rewrote some articles, especially older ones, resulting not only in fewer pages but also in better articles. This revised edition of the original, &ldquo;uncompressed&rdquo; series is based on the edits made for the compressed edition. However, we increased the font and image sizes and returned to a one-column layout for improved reading comfort. The book design is a collaborative effort by Laia Comellas, Marie Verdeil, and Johanna Gratzer. Marie Verdeil made the covers, Vaiva Vinskaitė did the typesetting. Image: The redesigned and revised chronological book edition. Photo: Marie Verdeil.

specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe

Hackers, Forklifts, and Other Things Manufacturers Blame on Repair

Repair.org · 2026-05-11 18:06 UTC

When lawmakers consider Right to Repair, manufacturers and their trade groups usually show up with the same script. They support repair, of course. They support consumer choice, naturally. They support small businesses, safety, sustainability, affordability, resilience, and probably puppies. They just oppose the actual law that would make repair possible. That script is on full display in Alaska, where HB 162 would give Alaskans more practical access to the parts, tools, and information needed to fix the products they own. And the opposition testimony has been revealing. Not because the arguments are new, but because they are so familiar, so exaggerated, and so openly hostile to the basic idea that anyone outside a manufacturer-controlled network can be trusted to repair anything. The message from industry is clear: repair is fine, as long as manufacturers get to decide who repairs, what gets repaired, when repair happens, and how much control they keep after the sale. That is not repair freedom. That is a service monopoly with better lighting.

Cisco Is Hiding Its Repair Monopoly Behind “Security”

Repair.org · 2026-05-04 16:20 UTC

It took years of pressure, but consumers and advocates forced Apple to let people fix their own phones. That fight is not over. It just moved. Now the targets include everything from McFlurry machines to John Deere tractors to enterprise hardware from Cisco Systems. And right now, Cisco is leading the pack in the race to be the least repair-friendly major OEM. Over the past two weeks in Colorado, Cisco, IBM, and Hewlett-Packard Enterprise helped unleash more than 20 lobbying firms to kill the right to repair for businesses and government. Their argument was simple. If you do not use OEM parts, you are putting national security at risk. This is not just wrong. It is fiction. Since the first right to repair bill in 2014, not a single real-world example has been produced to support this claim. Not one. No breach. No incident. No evidence. Just hypotheticals dressed up as policy. Instead, we get scenarios that sound like action movies, not reality. They also tried to argue that repair should be restricted for equipment used in nuclear facilities and other sensitive environments.
